5. Historical Data Collection

The observed indicator is based on precipitation measurements from thousands of land-based weather stations throughout the United States, collected using standard meteorological instruments. Altogether, NOAA’s nClimDiv data set incorporates data from more than 10,000 stations. These stations are spread among 344 climate divisions in the CONUS plus additional divisions in Alaska and Hawaii (although these have fewer years of data). Widespread, reliable data were available back to 1901 for the CONUS. The nClimDiv data set also incorporates a grid-based computational approach known as climatologically aided interpolation (Willmott & Robeson, 1995), which helps to address topographic variability. Data from individual stations are combined in a grid that covers the entire contiguous 48 states with 5-kilometer resolution. The technical documentation for the U.S. and Global Precipitation indicator provides more information, links, and supporting references for nClimDiv.

6. Indicator Derivation

Precipitation totals for this pairing’s graph are presented as anomalies. An anomaly represents the difference between an observed value and the corresponding value from a baseline period. This feature uses a baseline period of 1901–2000 for anomalies in the graph and a baseline of 1951–2000 for the percent changes shown in the maps.

Observed Data

NOAA calculated monthly and annual precipitation totals for each station, incorporating bias corrections as described in Section 9 below. They calculated anomalies in millimeters, which the project team converted to inches for accessibility.

To achieve uniform spatial coverage (i.e., not biased toward areas with a higher concentration of measuring stations), NOAA calculated area-weighted averages of grid-point estimates interpolated from station data. This made it possible to calculate a CONUS average for the graph.

The map shows long-term change in total precipitation over the CONUS for 1901–2023. This map is based on NOAA’s nClimDiv gridded analysis, with results averaged within each climate division. The slope of each precipitation trend was calculated from the annual climate division values by ordinary least-squares regression and then multiplied by the length of the entire period of record to get total change in inches. The total change was then converted to percent change, using average precipitation during the standard baseline period (1951–2000) as the denominator.

Model Outputs

The project team performed the following steps via R and Python scripts:

  • For each STAR-ESDM downscaled model, the team used the daily “pr” variable, converted millimeters to inches, and summed to get annual totals.
  • The project team calculated spatial averages for the CONUS (for the graph) and for individual climate divisions (for the map).
  • For the map, the team calculated percent change relative to the hindcast’s 1951–2000 mean.
  • The project team aggregated the 16 models using the standard Bayesian model weighting approach used in the Fifth National Climate Assessment and documented by Massoud et al. (2023).
  • For the plot, the team smoothed modeled results using an 11-year moving average. The team performed this step independently for the hindcast (through 2014) and for each scenario from 2015 (the first year of divergence) forward.

7. Alignment

To ensure consistency in how the anomalies are defined, the project team had to ensure that the observed and modeled anomalies were all presented relative to a common baseline. The observed CONUS anomalies for the graph had already been calculated with respect to a 1901–2000 baseline, as shown in the U.S. and Global Precipitation indicator. Downscaled model outputs were only available back to 1950, so the modeled anomalies were initially calculated relative to a standard 50-year baseline period: 1951–2000. The project team then shifted the model outputs vertically on the graph such that the 1951–2000 mean for the model hindcast would match the 1901–2000 mean for the observed time series. This aligns the model outputs with the observed anomalies that remain based on a 1901–2000 baseline. The alignment of baseline here is essentially just a vertical shift on the graph, not a change to the shape of the time series.

The maps show percent change, which cannot be adjusted with a simple vertical shift as was described above for anomalies in inches. Thus, the project team recalculated percent change for the observed data relative to the 1951–2000 mean, which was the same baseline used for the model outputs. This means the percent changes shown for the observed data here are not exactly the same as those shown in the U.S. and Global Precipitation indicator, where the CONUS is shown in relation to 1901–2000. However, the change in baseline led to only slight differences.

The results show good alignment. Thus, no other transformation was necessary.

8. Display

The interactive graph for this pairing shows the following elements:

  • Observed data from EPA’s indicator from 1901 to 2023.
  • Modeled hindcast from 1950 to 2014. The line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 16 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted from 1955 to 2009, as the project team did not attempt to apply any endpoint padding at either end of the series.
  • Modeled projections from 2015 to 2100 for four emissions scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5), with 2014 added for continuity (2014 is the last year before the scenarios diverge). Each scenario line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 16 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted starting at 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast annual ranges, although the scenarios do not start to diverge until 2015. Smoothed values for 2014–2019 pick up some hindcast years in the average. The 11-year means are plotted through 2095, including data from 2090 through 2100, the last year of available data. Scenarios have been assigned “plain-language” names for consistency throughout this pairings effort.
  • A shaded band around each of the scenarios reflects the 10th to 90th percentiles among the 16 models. This shaded band therefore illustrates the range of modeled values. The shaded bands show annual values; they have not been smoothed. The projected ranges start in 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast, but the scenarios begin to diverge in 2015.

The interactive maps show the following information by NOAA climate division:

  • Percent change over the entire observed period, based on total change (the linear regression slope multiplied by length of period) compared with the 1951–2000 average.
  • The projected percent change from 2024 to 2100, based on the same method, for each of the four emissions scenarios. Each map shows the Bayesian weighted average of all 16 models.

9. Quality Assurance and Quality Control

The technical documentation for the U.S. and Global Precipitation indicator discusses steps that NOAA takes to identify errors and biases in the data and to either remove these stations from the time series or apply correction factors. These steps address changes to station locations, methods, and instrumentation. Quality procedures for each GCM (e.g., validation) are described in source papers published by the organizations that have developed and run each model; these sources are available through links in the overall technical documentation [to be linked] for this effort. For each pairing, the project team conducted typical quality control steps including independently checking all aggregations, unit conversions, transformations, and other calculations.
